The Agile kangaroo rat (Dipodomys agilis) exhibits a suite of physiological and life history traits finely tuned to its arid environment. Male individuals ultimately reach an adult asymptotic body mass of 79 grams [Wwi = 79 grams], while females are slightly smaller, attaining a maximum adult weight of 78 grams [Wwi = 78 grams]; this modest sexual size dimorphism is characteristic of many heteromyid rodents. Field-reared neonates born to this species have a recorded wet weight at birth of 3.04 grams [Wwb = 3.04 grams], a value initially documented for the closely related desert kangaroo rat (Dipodomys deserti) but considered applicable for D. agilis given their similar reproductive allometry. The gestation period proceeds over approximately 25 days [tg = approximately 25 days] under stable thermal conditions of 35.3 °C [T = 35.3 °C], a duration reflecting the altricial developmental state of the offspring at parturition.

Reproductive output in the Agile kangaroo rat is modest but consistent with the species' semi-arid habitat and unpredictable resource base. Under the regulated ambient temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], females typically produce litters of 2.6 pups per litter [N_R_i = 2.6 pups per litter] and achieve a single litter annually [F_R_i = single litter annually]. This low annual fecundity is offset by a relatively extended lifespan compared to many other rodents of equivalent body size. The time from birth to weaning lasts approximately 25 days [tx = approximately 25 days] under the same thermal regime, after which the young begin to consume solid seeds and forage independently at a temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C].

Puberty, defined as the onset of gonadal maturation, is reached at 210 days after birth [tp = 210 days after birth] when the animals are maintained at 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C]. This protracted juvenile phase is notable for an animal of such small size and is thought to allow for the full development of the specialized craniodental and locomotor morphology required for efficient bipedal saltation and seed processing. During this post-weaning period, the growing juveniles transition from a dependence on maternal milk to a completely granivorous diet, storing seeds in external cheek pouches and caching them within their burrow systems. The comparatively late sexual maturation likely reflects the energetic constraints of a desert existence, where food availability is sporadic and the costs of reproduction are high. The ultimate adult body masses for both sexes are achieved prior to or concurrent with this reproductive activation.

Lifespan in the Agile kangaroo rat has been documented in captive settings, with the oldest recorded individuals surviving for approximately 6.2 years [am = approximately 6.2 years] under a stable temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C]. This is a remarkably long life for a rodent of its size, especially when compared to similarly sized muroid species, and it aligns with the slow life-history pace typical of heteromyids. This longevity is presumably linked to their efficient water conservation abilities and a lifestyle that minimizes exposure to predators via nocturnal activity and refuge in sealed burrows during the day. The maximum recorded age also contextualizes their reproductive strategy; with a single annual litter, a female could, over her lifetime, produce a modest number of offspring, assuming a gestation period of approximately 25 days [tg = approximately 25 days] at a temperature of 35.3 °C [T = 35.3 °C].

Basal metabolic rate provides further insight into the species' physiological adaptations. Respirometry measurements indicate a resting oxygen consumption of 63.6 milliliters per hour [JOi = 63.6 milliliters per hour] when the animal's body temperature is maintained at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This metabolic rate is relatively low for a mammal of its adult body mass, which ranges from 78 grams [Wwi = 78 grams] in females to 79 grams [Wwi = 79 grams] in males, a pattern that is congruent with the energetic economy required for survival in an environment where water and food are scarce. The low metabolic expenditure complements their behavioral traits, such as the daily torpor they can enter during cold nights, further reducing energy needs. This physiological conservatism underpins their ability to persist in chaparral and coastal sage scrub habitats of Southern California, where the management of energy and water budgets is paramount for long-term survival.
